L6  /  Pathological basis of oral & systemic disease

Pathology of Oral Infectious Disease

The mouth carries over 700 bacterial species plus fungi and viruses, and almost every infection here is a commensal that turned. Bacterial, prion, fungal and viral disease — and the clinical appearances you are expected to recognise on sight.

Lecturer
Dr Joseph Ryan
Sections
29
Slide plates
29
Builds on
L5 immunopathology
01

The oral microbiome

The mouth is not sterile, and that is the point.

The mouth carries a permanent, dense and diverse microbial population. The lecture opens here because every infection that follows is a disturbance of this community rather than an invasion of sterile territory.

Bacteria

>700 species

Including ultra-small bacteria of the ‘Candidate Phyla Radiation’ (CPR) group — organisms so small and so dependent on others that they were only recognised recently.

Fungi

Chiefly Candida

Present as a commensal in a large proportion of healthy mouths.

Viruses

Persistent and latent

Most adults carry several herpesviruses for life after a childhood primary infection.

Why >700 species matters

Because it means presence is not disease. Finding Candida or Actinomyces in a mouth tells you almost nothing on its own — both are normal residents. The clinical question is never “is the organism there?” but “why has it started causing harm?”

02

Commensal, opportunist, acute, latent

Two axes that organise the whole lecture.

Axis 1

Commensalism vs opportunistic infection

The same organism can live harmlessly on the host (commensal) or cause disease when the host’s defences change (opportunistic infection).

Axis 2

Acute vs latent disease

Some infections run a short course and resolve. Others become latent — the organism persists silently and can reactivate later.

Straight from Lecture 5C

Opportunistic infection is the clinical face of immunodeficiency. Everything Part 3 said about HIV and about immunosuppressed transplant patients turns up here as oral disease — candidosis, hairy leukoplakia, herpes, Kaposi’s sarcoma. Same principle, seen in the tissue you examine.

A patient has Candida cultured from a swab. Does that make the diagnosis?

No. Candida is a normal commensal of the mouth, so a positive culture alone shows only carriage. The lecture is explicit that no single test reliably discriminates the transition from candidal saprophytism to pathogenicity. Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture, and management rests on identifying what changed about the host to allow the commensal to become an opportunist.

03

How oral infections are classified

Four groups, and how bacteria are sorted within them.

Purpose of a classification

To provide a natural framework for the organization of the diversity of life.

The four groups of oral microbial infection

GroupCovered in this lecture
BacterialActinomycosis, syphilis, tuberculosis
PrionsCreutzfeldt–Jakob disease
FungiCandidosis — in its several forms
VirusesHerpes viruses, Coxsackie, mumps, HPV, HIV, hepatitis C

How oral bacteria are classified

The majority of oral bacteria are classified by their morphology, depending on:

  1. Staining and enzyme tests
    Gram staining, catalase, haemolysis and coagulase test.
  2. Shape
    Cocci, bacilli or spirochaetes.
  3. Oxygen requirement
    Aerobic, anaerobic or facultative anaerobes.
  4. Arrangement or spore formation
    Whether cocci grow in clusters or pairs/chains, or whether bacilli produce spores.
Why this scaffolding is worth keeping

Each bacterial disease below is introduced by exactly these features. Actinomycosis is Gram-positive, branching, anaerobic; TB is an acid-fast, non-sporing bacillus that will not take the Gram stain at all. If you hold the four criteria, the descriptions stop being lists to memorise and become answers to the same four questions.

From the lecture slides
04

Actinomycosis

A commensal that burrows — and the reason it is called lumpy jaw.

OrganismGram positive, branching, anaerobic or micro-aerophilic bacteria
SpeciesActinomyces israelii, A. naeslundii, A. viscosus, A. odontolyticus
Normal habitatCommensals of the mouth and GI tract
SpreadUsually by direct extension, with a tendency to form sinuses and fistulae
Two signature findings

“Sulphur granules” — colonies of actinomyces and filaments surrounded by neutrophils. Yellow granules in the discharging pus, and they are diagnostic.

“Lumpy jaw” — the most common presentation is a chronic soft tissue swelling which leads to a hard, board-like lesion with a lumpy appearance.

Sinuses — back to Lecture 3B

You defined a sinus as an abnormal track from a cavity or abscess to a body surface. Actinomycosis is the classic organism for producing them, because it spreads by direct extension through tissue planes rather than via lymphatics or blood. That is also why it crosses anatomical boundaries that other infections respect.

A patient has a hard, board-like swelling of the jaw discharging pus through a skin sinus, with yellow granules in the discharge. What is the diagnosis and what are the granules?

Actinomycosis — the classic “lumpy jaw” presentation, following chronic soft tissue swelling. The granules are “sulphur granules”: colonies of actinomyces and filaments surrounded by neutrophils. The sinus reflects its spread by direct extension, with a tendency to form sinuses and fistulae.

From the lecture slides
05

Spirochaetes and ANUG

Spiral organisms, and the three diseases they cause.

Spirochaetes

Spiral, motile organisms with a central protoplasmic cylinder.

The oral treponemes are T. denticola, T. vincentii, T. scoliodontium, T. orale, T. pectinovarum, T. socranskii and T. macrodentium.

DiseaseOrganism
ANUG (acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis)T. vincentii
Periodontal diseaseT. denticola
SyphilisT. pallidum
Learn the three pairs together

Vincentii → ANUG. Denticola → periodontal disease. Pallidum → syphilis. Three treponemes, three very different diseases — and only one of them is a sexually transmitted systemic infection.

ANUG in context

Necrotising ulcerative gingivitis reappears twice more in this lecture — in the HIV oral manifestations list, alongside necrotising ulcerative periodontitis and linear gingival erythema. Its presence in a young, otherwise healthy-looking patient is a reason to think about underlying immunosuppression.

From the lecture slides
06

Syphilis

Four stages, each with its own oral presentation.

Caused by Treponema pallidum. The oral manifestations differ by stage, and the lecture tabulates them.

StageIntraoral manifestations
PrimaryA chancre involving sites such as tongue, gingivae or lips; regional lymphadenopathy may be observed
SecondaryRaised lesions with a pseudomembrane surrounded by erythema (mucous patches) and/or snail track oral mucosal ulceration, with regional lymphadenopathy
LatentOften no clinical manifestations. However, so-called mucocutaneous relapse with nonspecific oral mucosal white patches may occur
TertiaryGumma — a crater-type ulcer that may involve bone, typically the hard palate. White patches may develop intra-orally (syphilitic leukoplakia), reported as potentially malignant lesions
Syphilitic leukoplakia is potentially malignant

The white patches of tertiary syphilis have been reported as potentially malignant lesions. A white patch is never simply cosmetic, and this is one of several causes in this lecture — chronic hyperplastic candidosis is another.

A crater-type ulcer perforating the hard palate. Which stage of syphilis, and what is the lesion called?

Tertiary syphilis, and the lesion is a gumma — a crater-type ulcer that may involve bone, typically the hard palate. The same stage may also produce syphilitic leukoplakia, which is regarded as potentially malignant.

From the lecture slides
07

Tuberculosis

A global killer, with an oral presentation you will rarely see.

The scale

Previously an invariably fatal disease. It remains the second most common infectious cause of death in adults worldwide and the leading killer of HIV-positive people. 1 in 4 people in the world has latent TB, with a 5–15% risk of falling ill.

Spread is by inhalation of aerosol droplets.

The organism

  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis
  • Acid and alcohol fast, slender, non-sporing bacilli
  • Does not take up the Gram stain, because of long chain fatty acids in the cell wall (mycolic acid)
  • Demonstrated instead with the Ziehl–Neelsen or Kinyoun stain

The disease

A chronic infection characterised by the formation of granulomas. The primary site is usually the lung. Oral lesions occur in <1%, thought to arise by implantation from coughing: variable presentation, but usually painless ulceration on the dorsum of the tongue.

Treatment

Combination therapy for 6 months:

Isoniazid Rifampicin Pyrazinamide Ethambutol
Two threads from earlier lectures

TB is the archetypal caseating granuloma from Lecture 3B — the response to an organism the body cannot destroy. It is also a type IV hypersensitivity reaction from Lecture 5A: the granuloma is sustained by Th1 cells releasing IFN-γ to activate macrophages. The tissue damage in TB is largely the immune response, not the bacillus.

Why the Gram stain fails

Mycolic acid in the cell wall. The same waxy coat that blocks the Gram stain is what makes the organism acid and alcohol fast — once stained by Ziehl–Neelsen it resists decolourisation. One structural feature explains both the negative and the positive test.

Why can't M. tuberculosis be identified with a Gram stain, and what is used instead?

Because of long chain fatty acids — mycolic acid — in the cell wall, which prevent uptake of the Gram stain. The Ziehl–Neelsen or Kinyoun stain is used instead, exploiting the fact that the organism is acid and alcohol fast: the same waxy wall that blocks Gram staining prevents the ZN stain being washed out by acid alcohol.

From the lecture slides
08

Prions and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease

Not an organism at all — an infectious protein.

Prion

‘Proteinaceous infectious particle’ — derived from a protease-sensitive protein which is a constituent of the normal cell membrane.

CJD belongs to a family of human and animal diseases known as the transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs) or prion diseases. Spongiform refers to the characteristic appearance of infected brains, which become filled with holes until they resemble sponges under the microscope.

Acquired CJD

Medical transmission

Transmitted by exposure to brain or nervous system tissue, usually through certain medical procedures.

Variant CJD

Dietary transmission

A subset of acquired CJD, acquired by eating meat from cattle affected by bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) — commonly, “mad cow” disease.

Why this appears in a dental lecture

Prions are not destroyed by standard autoclaving, and acquired CJD is transmitted through medical procedures involving neural tissue. It is the reason instrument decontamination protocols exist in the form they do — the ordinary sterilisation assumptions that hold for bacteria and viruses do not hold here.

The conceptual point

A prion has no nucleic acid. It is a normal cell membrane protein in a misfolded form that induces the same misfolding in its neighbours. That is why it sits in its own category alongside bacteria, fungi and viruses rather than within any of them.

09

Candida: species, testing and predisposition

The commonest oral fungal infection, and why it starts.

Species encountered in human infections

C. albicans C. tropicalis C. glabrata C. parapsilosis C. stellatoidea C. krusei C. kefyr

Testing for Candida

Culture Swab Swirl DNA PCR Smear + PAS stain
What no test can tell you

“No convincing evidence of a single test or method better able to discriminate the transition from candidal saprophytism to pathogenicity has been reported in the literature.”

In other words, laboratory testing confirms Candida is present. It cannot tell you whether it is causing the disease in front of you. That judgement stays clinical.

Predisposition to candidal pathogenicity

Drugs

Immune modulatory medications

Corticosteroids especially — including inhaled.

Haematological

Blood dyscrasias and malignancy

 

Diet

Dietary factors

Including the deficiencies that also cause angular cheilitis.

Endocrine

Endocrine disorders

Diabetes above all.

Immune

Immunologic disorders

Both primary and acquired.

Saliva

Salivary changes

Reduced flow removes a major defence.

The six categories are the treatment plan

First-line treatment for oral candidosis is remove the predisposing factors. That means this list is not background — it is the checklist you work through before reaching for an antifungal.

10

Classifying oral candidosis

Three classifications, and why the newest drops acute and chronic.

Early classificationRevised (1990)Proposed
Acute pseudomembranousAcute pseudomembranousPseudomembranous
—Chronic pseudomembranous
Acute atrophicAcute erythematousErythematous
Chronic atrophicChronic erythematous
Chronic hyperplasticChronic nodular / chronic plaque-likeHyperplastic
(Denture stomatitis)(Denture-associated candidosis)(Denture-associated stomatitis)
Angular cheilitisCandida-associated cheilitisAngular cheilitis
Why the terms changed

The early classification tied each form to a time course — acute or chronic. That broke down once chronic pseudomembranous candidosis was recognised, since pseudomembranous disease was supposed to be acute by definition. The proposed classification therefore drops the time qualifier altogether and names the forms by appearance: pseudomembranous, erythematous, hyperplastic.

Expect all three sets in the literature

Older texts say “acute atrophic candidosis”; newer ones say “erythematous”. They are the same disease. The lecture presents all three columns deliberately, and knowing the synonyms is what stops a question tripping you.

From the lecture slides
11

Pseudomembranous candidosis

Thrush — the form everyone pictures.

  • Nonadherent creamy white patches or flecks
  • Easily wiped — the defining feature
  • Underlying mucosa erythematous and bleeding
  • Rarely painful
  • Commonly affected areas: soft palate, oropharynx, tongue, cheek, gingivae
What the pseudomembrane actually is

A mesh of fungal hyphae containing entangled desquamated epithelial cells, fibrin, keratin, necrotic tissue and bacteria. That composition is why it lifts off — it sits on the mucosa rather than being part of it.

Who gets it

Immunocompromised individuals, and specifically:

Extremes of ageInfants and the elderly
Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus 
HIV infection and AIDS 
Therapeutically immunocompromisedEspecially corticosteroids
Antipsychotics, anticholinergicsVia reduced salivary flow
Long-term broad-spectrum antibioticsSuppressing the competing bacterial flora
Two different mechanisms in that list

Antipsychotics and anticholinergics act by drying the mouth — removing saliva as a defence. Broad-spectrum antibiotics act by removing the bacterial competition, letting a fungus that was always present overgrow. Neither drug suppresses immunity; both still produce candidosis. That is the commensal-to-opportunist shift in two forms.

From the lecture slides
12

Erythematous candidosis

Red, not white — and easily missed.

  • Localised erythema of the oral mucosa
  • May or may not be painful
  • Commonly affected areas: dorsal tongue and palate; buccal mucosa less common

Associations

Chronic broad-spectrum antibiotics Chronic corticosteroids HIV infection
Why this one gets missed

There is nothing white to see. A patient with a sore, red tongue and no plaque does not look like “thrush”, and erythematous candidosis is easily written off as irritation. It was formerly called acute atrophic or chronic atrophic candidosis — the same disease under three names.

Back to Lecture 5C

Erythematous candidosis was the first item in the HIV oral manifestations list in Immunodeficiency, and it heads the worldwide HIV list later in this lecture. Unexplained erythematous candidosis in a young adult is a reason to think about undiagnosed immunosuppression.

From the lecture slides
13

Chronic hyperplastic candidosis

The white patch that will not come off — and the one to worry about.

  • White lesion that cannot be removed
  • Well demarcated, slightly elevated
  • Progresses from small translucent to large, dense opaque plaques
  • Commonly affected areas: post-commissural buccal mucosa, tongue, palate posterior to upper dentures
  • Patient may be a smoker, and typically >35 years of age
Once called candidal leukoplakia

The older name tells you why this form matters. Unlike the other two, it is a persistent white patch in a group of patients who often smoke — and it cannot be distinguished from other white patches by wiping it.

Yeast carriage and epithelial dysplasia

Oral yeast carriage has been shown to correlate with the presence and degree of oral epithelial dysplasia. The lecture poses the causal question without resolving it:

Possibility 1

Yeast first

Did the chronic presence of yeast and associated inflammation lead to a dysplastic change?

Possibility 2

Dysplasia first

Was it dysplasia or carcinoma to begin with, and the yeast came later?

The clinical consequence is the same either way

Whichever direction the causation runs, a non-removable white patch associated with Candida sits alongside epithelial dysplasia. Treating the fungus does not settle whether the epithelium is dysplastic — which is why this lesion, unlike the other two forms, raises the question of biopsy.

Two patients have white patches on the buccal mucosa. One wipes off, one does not. How does your management differ?

The one that wipes off is pseudomembranous candidosis — a mesh of hyphae, desquamated cells, fibrin, keratin and bacteria sitting on the mucosa. Manage by identifying and removing the predisposing factor.

The one that does not may be chronic hyperplastic candidosis, formerly called candidal leukoplakia, typically post-commissural, in a patient over 35 who may smoke. Because yeast carriage correlates with the presence and degree of epithelial dysplasia, and because the differential for a persistent white patch includes dysplasia and carcinoma, this one warrants further investigation rather than antifungal treatment alone.

From the lecture slides
14

Chronic mucocutaneous candidosis

A genetic immune fault that shows in the mouth first.

Definition

A heterogeneous group of syndromes with common features including chronic noninvasive Candida infections of the skin, nails and mucous membranes, with associated autoimmune manifestations — most commonly endocrinopathies.

  • Caused by genetic faults in the immune system
  • Identified early in life
  • May include oral candidosis
  • Oral lesions often precede skin and nail involvement
Why the dentist matters here

Oral lesions often precede skin and nail involvement. In a child with persistent, recurring candidosis, the mouth may show the disease before anything else does — and the underlying problem is a primary immune defect, not poor hygiene.

Both halves of Lecture 5 in one condition

Chronic mucocutaneous candidosis pairs a primary immunodeficiency (Part 3) with autoimmune endocrinopathies (Part 2). Failure of immune regulation produces too little response against Candida and too much against self, simultaneously.

15

Candida-related conditions

Five presentations where Candida is implicated — with a caveat.

Denture-associated stomatitis

Erythema and oedema restricted to the denture supporting area. May be related to:

Poor oral and denture hygiene Nocturnal denture wearing Loose dentures
The diagnostic clue is the outline

The erythema is restricted to the denture supporting area — it stops exactly where the denture stops. That sharp correspondence to the fitting surface is what distinguishes it from other causes of palatal redness.

Palatal papillary hyperplasia

A characteristic papillary reactive inflammatory lesion of the hard palate that generally develops under a denture. Common in:

Habitual mouth breathers High palatal vault Ill-fitting dentures Night-time denture wear Poor denture hygiene

Median rhomboid glossitis

  • Symmetrical, erythematous, elliptical or rhomboid-like area
  • On the posterior dorsal surface of the tongue, just anterior to the circumvallate papillae
  • Atrophy of the filiform papillae
  • Associated with smoking and the use of inhaled steroids — there may be an opposing lesion on the palate
The kissing lesion

Where the tongue lesion has a matching patch on the palate, the two are in contact at rest. Seeing both together is strong support for the diagnosis, and points at inhaled steroids as the cause — which makes rinsing after inhaler use the relevant advice.

Angular cheilitis

  • Erythematous fissuring at one or both corners of the mouth
  • Often also intra-oral candidal infection
  • Also commonly associated with staphylococci and streptococci
  • Driven by a chronically moist environment — from loss of OVD or wrinkling, or lip licking
  • Seen in iron deficiency anaemia and vitamin B12 deficiency
Angular cheilitis is a sign, not a diagnosis

It points three ways at once: a local cause (loss of occlusal vertical dimension creating a moist fold), a microbial one (Candida plus staphylococci and streptococci — so it is often not purely fungal), and a systemic one (iron deficiency anaemia and B12 deficiency). Treating the corners of the mouth without asking why they are wet, or checking for anaemia, misses the actual problem.

Linear gingival erythema

Defined as a non-plaque-induced localised or generalised gingivitis presenting as a distinct erythematous band of 2–3 mm along the margin of the gingivae. It is likely that mixed fungal and bacterial opportunistic infections are responsible.

The lecturer's caveat — read it carefully

On median rhomboid glossitis and palatal papillary hyperplasia: “conclusive evidence of a direct aetiopathogenic relationship between MRG and PPH and candidal infection has not been found”.

These are Candida-related conditions, which is not the same as Candida-caused. The association is real; the causation is not established.

From the lecture slides
16

Treating oral candidosis

Remove the cause first. Antifungals are second line.

First line — remove predisposing factors

  1. Denture hygiene
    Remove the denture at night, clean it, then leave it out to dry. Soak in 1% sodium hypochlorite once a week for acrylic dentures; soak in chlorhexidine once a week for chrome dentures.
  2. Adequate oral hygiene
    Including chlorhexidine mouthwash.
  3. Rinse the mouth after using steroid inhalers
    Removing the drug that is suppressing local defence.
  4. Smoking cessation
    Relevant to hyperplastic candidosis and median rhomboid glossitis alike.
Why the denture goes in different solutions

Sodium hypochlorite for acrylic, chlorhexidine for chrome. Hypochlorite corrodes cobalt-chromium, so it is reserved for acrylic-only dentures. Getting this the wrong way round damages the patient’s denture.

Second line — antifungal treatment

Used in selected cases if removing predisposing factors does not prove to be successful.

DrugRegimen
Miconazole
(Daktarin oral gel)		2% gel, 2.5 mL orally (half a teaspoon), 4 times daily, after meals, for 14 to 21 days
Amphotericin B10 mg lozenge sucked, 4 times daily for 14 to 21 days
Nystatin10 mg lozenge sucked, 4 times daily for 14 to 21 days, or oral drops 1 mL, 4 times daily for 14 to 21 days
Miconazole and warfarin — a genuine danger

Miconazole can potentiate the effect of warfarin. A topical oral gel is easy to regard as harmless, but enough is absorbed to raise INR and cause bleeding. The lecture also warns to be careful with statins. Check the medical history before prescribing it — this is a prescription a dentist writes routinely, and the interaction is easy to overlook.

Candidaemia and invasive candidosis

Infections caused by Candida spp. are most frequently localised and superficial. But in severely immunocompromised patients, candidosis can be systemic — invasive candidosis — and is associated with high mortality. The same commensal that causes a wipe-off white patch in a healthy mouth can be lethal when defences fail completely.

A patient on warfarin has denture stomatitis. What is your first-line management, and what must you avoid?

First line is removing the predisposing factors, not prescribing: improve denture hygiene (remove at night, clean, leave out to dry, soak weekly — 1% sodium hypochlorite for acrylic, chlorhexidine for chrome), improve oral hygiene, and address any denture fit problem.

Avoid miconazole, which potentiates warfarin and risks bleeding. If an antifungal proves necessary, nystatin or amphotericin lozenges avoid that interaction.

17

Herpesviruses and latency

Eight of them, and one mechanism that explains recurrence.

The eight human herpesviruses

No.VirusPrincipal oral relevance
1Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1)Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis; herpes labialis
2Herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2)Genital; occasionally oral
3Varicella zoster virus (VZV)Chickenpox; shingles
4Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)Infectious mononucleosis; oral hairy leukoplakia
5Cytomegalovirus (CMV)Atypical oral ulcers; periodontal disease
6HHV-6Roseola infantum
7HHV-7Roseola infantum
8HHV-8Kaposi’s sarcoma
How common they are

Other than HSV-2 and HHV-8, most adults (over 90%) have circulating antibodies to each of these viruses — so they have had the primary infection at some stage. Most were probably sub-clinical and transient, and occurred during the first 3 years of life.

The latency mechanism

  1. Initial infection
    Viral particles replicate and are released from mucosal cells as they rupture. These travel up nerve cells and the viral DNA is incorporated into the nucleus of the nerve cell.
  2. Latency
    Viral DNA lies latent in the cell nucleus — for example, in the trigeminal nucleus.
  3. Secondary infection
    When a precipitating factor occurs (e.g. stress or illness), the viral particles start replicating and travel down the nerve to the nerve endings, and infect mucosal cells.
Why treatment is given in the prodrome

Antivirals block replication. By the time vesicles have formed, replication has largely happened and the damage is done — so aciclovir applied at the ulcer stage achieves little. This is why the instruction is always “start at the first tingle”.

From the lecture slides
18

Herpes simplex virus 1

Primary gingivostomatitis in childhood, cold sores thereafter.

Primary

Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis

  • Usually in childhood
  • Transmission by direct contact or saliva
  • Incubation 5–10 days
  • Prodrome: malaise, fever, headache, lymphadenopathy
  • Small rupturing vesicles over all oral mucosa
  • Very painful
  • Resolution 7–10 days
  • Treatment: ensure fluids and pain relief until symptoms resolve
Reactivation

Herpes labialis

  • Affects 30–40% of the population at some time during life
  • Precipitants: sunlight; stress — psychological and physiological; hormonal
  • Location: mucocutaneous junctions
  • Sequence: prodrome → reddening → vesiculation → pustule → ulcer
  • 5–10 days
  • Treatment in the prodrome: aciclovir cream 5%, 4-hourly
The whole-mouth clue

Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis affects all oral mucosa, including keratinised tissue and gingivae, with systemic upset. Recurrent disease is confined to mucocutaneous junctions. Distribution separates them, and both differ from herpangina, which spares the gingivae.

Fluids matter more than they sound

The treatment for primary gingivostomatitis is fluids and pain relief — because a small child with very painful ulceration across the entire mouth will stop drinking. Dehydration, not the virus, is the reason these children are admitted.

From the lecture slides
19

Varicella zoster virus

Chickenpox, then shingles — and two named complications.

Primary

Chickenpox

  • Cutaneous rash with vesicles and pustules
  • Fever and malaise; highly contagious
  • After 3–4 days pustules form scabs
  • Oral findings: short-lasting small white-opaque vesicles that rupture and ulcerate, usually on palate and buccal mucosa
  • Primarily in school-aged children
  • Diagnosed on clinical history; treatment symptomatic, same as HSV
  • Forms latency by the same mechanism as HSV-1
Reactivation

Shingles

  • Unilateral dermatomal distribution of vesicles/ulcers
  • Prodrome before rash — burning, itching, prickling
  • Likes trigeminal — ophthalmic division most common
  • Risk of conjunctival keratosis
  • Middle to late life; immunodeficiency
Unilateral and stopping at the midline

Shingles follows a dermatome, so the lesions stop abruptly at the midline. In the mouth that is unmistakable and is the single most useful distinguishing feature from HSV, which respects no such boundary.

Two named complications

Complication 1

Ramsay Hunt syndrome

Involves the chorda tympani (VII). Produces vesicles/ulcers of the external ear (otitis externa), anterior two-thirds of the tongue, soft palate, and facial palsy.

Complication 2

Post-herpetic neuralgia

Affects >30% of patients with shingles — persistent neuropathic pain in the affected dermatome after the rash has gone.

Facial palsy with ear vesicles

Ramsay Hunt syndrome is the reason a facial palsy should prompt you to look in the ear and at the tongue. A palsy with vesicles is not Bell’s palsy — it is zoster, and the distinction changes management.

Unilateral vesicles on the palate stopping sharply at the midline, in a 70-year-old with burning pain preceding the rash. Diagnosis?

Shingles — reactivation of varicella zoster virus. The features are all characteristic: unilateral dermatomal distribution, a prodrome of burning, itching or prickling before the rash, and onset in middle to late life. VZV likes the trigeminal nerve, and over 30% of shingles patients develop post-herpetic neuralgia.

From the lecture slides
20

Cytomegalovirus and Epstein–Barr virus

Two herpesviruses with distinctive oral consequences.

Cytomegalovirus

  • Primary: an infectious mononucleosis-like syndrome
  • Cytomegalic inclusion disease — widespread calcification
  • Reactivation in immunosuppression: pneumonia, colitis, encephalitis and chorioretinitis
  • Oral association: atypical oral ulcers; periodontal disease

Epstein–Barr virus: infectious mononucleosis

  • Teenagers / young adults
  • Salivary transmission — “the kissing disease”
  • Long incubation time (35+ days)
  • Pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, malaise, arthralgia, myalgia

Epstein–Barr virus: oral hairy leukoplakia

  • An EBV-related epithelial proliferation
  • Bilateral: dorsum of tongue, lateral border of tongue, floor of mouth
  • Occurs in immunosuppression: HIV disease, ciclosporin, corticosteroids, diabetes mellitus

Other EBV-associated malignancies

Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma Burkitt’s lymphoma Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Hairy leukoplakia, seen twice

This is the same lesion from Lecture 5C’s HIV oral manifestations. Note what this lecture adds: it is not exclusive to HIV — ciclosporin, corticosteroids and diabetes also produce it. It signals immunosuppression, of which HIV is one cause.

A third white patch that will not rub off

Hairy leukoplakia joins chronic hyperplastic candidosis and syphilitic leukoplakia on the list of non-removable white patches in this lecture. Distribution helps: hairy leukoplakia is bilateral and favours the lateral tongue.

From the lecture slides
21

HHV-6, HHV-7 and HHV-8

Two trivial, one malignant.

HHV-6 & 7

Roseoloviruses

  • Approaching 100% seroprevalence
  • Primary infection: roseola infantum
  • Mild pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy and fever
  • Self-limiting
  • Replicates in the salivary glands and is shed in saliva
HHV-8

Kaposi’s sarcoma herpesvirus

  • Kaposi’s sarcoma — a malignant neoplasm of lymphatic endothelial cells
  • Primary infection → resides in endothelial cells
  • Immunosuppression allows for proliferation
  • Most common neoplasm in HIV-positive individuals
The pattern from Lecture 5

HHV-8 behaves exactly as Lecture 5C described: a virus held in check by immune surveillance, which produces a tumour once that surveillance is lost. The same logic explained the 40× malignancy rate in transplant patients in Part 2 — and Kaposi’s sarcoma appeared in both settings for the same reason.

Shed in saliva

HHV-6 and 7 replicate in the salivary glands and are shed in saliva. That, plus near-universal seroprevalence, explains why almost everyone acquires them in early childhood — and it is the same transmission route as EBV’s “kissing disease”.

From the lecture slides
22

Coxsackie virus

Herpangina and hand, foot and mouth — and telling them from herpes.

Coxsackievirus belongs to a family of nonenveloped, linear, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses, Picornaviridae, genus Enterovirus — which also includes poliovirus and echovirus.

Presentation 1

Herpangina

  • Fever and sore throat usually last two days
  • Followed by numerous small vesicles, 1–2 mm, found mostly on the pillar of fauces, uvula, tonsils and palate (3–4 days)
Presentation 2

Hand, foot and mouth disease

  • Preschool outbreak
  • Incubation 2–6 days
  • Small vesicles on the oral mucosa
  • Plus palmar surfaces of the hands and plantar surfaces of the feet
How to tell these from primary herpetic gingivostomatitis

The lecture gives a distinguishing feature for each:

  • Herpangina — the gingivae are not commonly affected, and there are no recurrences: eradication + immunity.
  • Hand, foot and mouth — the extra-oral lesions help distinguish it from herpetic gingivostomatitis.
A preschool child has oral vesicles during a nursery outbreak. What two features would point away from primary herpetic gingivostomatitis?

Lesions on the palms and soles — the extra-oral lesions help distinguish hand, foot and mouth disease from herpetic gingivostomatitis. And if the lesions were confined to the fauces, uvula, tonsils and palate with the gingivae spared, that points to herpangina. Both are Coxsackie virus, and neither recurs — there is eradication and immunity, unlike HSV which becomes latent.

From the lecture slides
23

Measles and mumps

Two paramyxoviruses, both vaccine-preventable.

Morbillivirus

Measles

  • RNA virus; incubation 10–12 days
  • Infectious from 2 days before symptoms until 4 days after the rash appears
  • Prodrome: fever, malaise, coryza, conjunctivitis and cough
  • Koplik spots — red spots with blue-white specks on the buccal mucosa
  • Followed by an exanthematous rash initially involving the face
  • Vaccine — MMR
Rubulavirus

Mumps

  • Bilateral swelling of the parotid salivary gland
  • Occasionally submandibular, unilateral
  • Incubation 14–21 days
  • Malaise, anorexia, fever and sialadenitis
  • Normal saliva despite ductal inflammation
  • Vaccine — MMR
Koplik spots come first

Koplik spots appear on the buccal mucosa during the prodrome — before the skin rash. A dentist examining a febrile child could in principle make the diagnosis before the measles rash exists, at a point when the patient is already infectious.

Normal saliva in mumps

Despite florid ductal inflammation, the saliva is normal — not purulent. That distinguishes mumps from bacterial sialadenitis, where pus can be expressed from the duct. Bilateral parotid swelling in an unvaccinated child with clear saliva is mumps.

24

Human papillomavirus: the lesions

Four oral presentations, each with its own types.

HPV is a group of DNA viruses with about 200 identified sub-types, classified by tissue tropism into dermatotropic and mucosotropic. It is typically transmitted by direct contact with an infected lesion.

How common

  • Female lifetime risk of infection 50–80%
  • 10–15% of women fail to mount an adequate T-cell response and develop persistent infection
  • Oral HPV (NHANES 2011–2014, adults 18–69): any type — males 11.5%, women 3.2%; high risk (HPV 16 or 18) — males 7.3%
LesionHPV typesFeatures
Squamous papilloma6 and 11Most common oral form. Finger-like projections giving a rough or cauliflower-like surface; white or pink depending on keratinisation; generally a single lesion; no symptoms and no known malignant potential
Verruca vulgaris1 and 57Generally a skin wart (common on hands) but can present orally; clinical and histological appearance same as squamous papilloma
Condyloma acuminatum2, 6 and 11Commonly genital warts, found orally following sexual transmission — through oral sex. Presents as multiple viral warts
Multifocal epithelial hyperplasia
(Heck’s disease)		13 and 32Multiple soft, flat or rounded elevated nodules, same colour as mucosa or whitish; lesions seem to disappear when the mucosa is stretched; buccal and labial mucosa

Treatment for all four is surgical removal — for Heck’s disease, if required, for aesthetic reasons.

Heck's disease — the stretch sign

When the involved mucosa is stretched, the lesions seem to disappear. That is a free clinical test needing no equipment. It is found in children living in unhygienic and crowded conditions, with higher prevalence in First Nations and Indigenous Australian populations, and it develops early in childhood and seems to regress with age.

Two lesions that look identical

Verruca vulgaris has the same clinical and histological appearance as squamous papilloma. They are separated by HPV type (1 and 57 versus 6 and 11) and by the usual site — verruca vulgaris is normally a hand wart. You cannot tell them apart down a microscope.

From the lecture slides
25

HPV and head and neck cancer

The numbers, and why you palpate lymph nodes.

Oropharyngeal cancers that are HPV positive40–80%
Most common sitesBase of tongue, tonsils
Types most associatedHPV 16, 18, 31 and 33 — 90% are HPV 16
Role in cancers of the oral cavityLittle to none — ~3.6%
Oropharynx is not oral cavity

This distinction is the whole point of the section. HPV drives 40–80% of oropharyngeal cancer but only about 3.6% of oral cavity cancer. The oropharynx means base of tongue and tonsils — behind the area you can inspect easily. Confusing the two sites makes the statistics meaningless.

Why we palpate lymph nodes

HPV-related oropharyngeal tumours often present with an enlarged mass in the neck — the lecture’s own emphasis. The primary is hidden at the tongue base or tonsil, so the first detectable sign is the node. Neck palpation is not a formality; for this cancer it may be the only way it is picked up.

Vaccination

The same HPV subtypes cause cervical cancer and are targeted by the Gardasil vaccine. Gardasil now targets HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58.

Note what the vaccine covers

The list includes both the low-risk types causing warts (6, 11) and the high-risk oncogenic types (16, 18, 31, 33). A vaccine given for cervical cancer prevention therefore also covers the types driving oropharyngeal cancer — which is why the programme matters to dentistry.

A patient presents with a neck mass and no visible oral lesion. Why does HPV make this presentation likely, and where would you suspect the primary?

40–80% of oropharyngeal cancers are HPV positive, and the most common sites are the base of tongue and tonsils — areas not readily visible on routine oral examination. These tumours often present with an enlarged mass in the neck, which is the lecture’s stated reason for palpating lymph nodes. HPV 16 accounts for 90% of these. Note that HPV has little to no role in cancers of the oral cavity proper (~3.6%).

From the lecture slides
26

HIV

Global and Australian figures, transmission, and prevention.

The scale

  • Approximately 37.9 million people living with HIV at the end of 2018, with 1.7 million newly infected in 2017 globally
  • The WHO African Region is the most affected — 25.7 million people living with HIV in 2018, accounting for almost two thirds of the global total

In Australia

Estimated HIV positive (end 2017)27,545
Unaware they were HIV positive2,899
Prevalence — gay and bisexual men7.9%
Prevalence — people who inject drugs0.7%
Prevalence — Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander people0.11%
Prevalence — all adults in Australia0.14%

Course of infection

  1. Transmission
    Sexual intercourse; parenteral; vertical.
  2. Primary infection
    “Flu-like” — acute seroconversion syndrome.
  3. Chronic carriage
    Of the HIV virus.
  4. Opportunistic infections
    Related to CD4+ lymphocyte dysfunction.
  5. AIDS
    Acquired immune deficiency syndrome.

Incidence and mortality are falling

By the end of 2017: 1.8 million newly diagnosed (down from 3.1 million in 2000); 21.7 million people had access to HIV treatments (up from 7.5 million in 2010 and 17 million in 2015); 940,000 people died of AIDS-related causes — a reduction of 47%.

Combination antiretroviral drugs (cART)

NRTI / NtRTI — ‘nukes’ NNRTIs — ‘non-nukes’ Protease inhibitors Integrase inhibitors Entry inhibitors

Reducing transmission

PrEP

Pre-exposure prophylaxis

Regular use of HIV medications by HIV-negative people to prevent HIV acquisition — tenofovir + emtricitabine.

PEP

Post-exposure prophylaxis

A 28-day course following accidental exposure. Must be commenced within 72 hours.

U=U

Undetectable = Untransmittable

The Opposites Attract study followed 343 gay couples of differing HIV status and found no HIV transmission in 16,889 acts of condomless anal sex where the HIV-positive partner was on fully suppressive treatment.

PEP is time-critical — 72 hours

This is the number to carry. After a needlestick or other occupational exposure, post-exposure prophylaxis must be commenced within 72 hours and runs for 28 days. Reporting an injury promptly is what makes it possible.

Lecture 5C gave the mechanism

Immunodeficiency explained why HIV does this: gp120 binding CD4, with CXCR4 and CCR5 co-receptors, destroying the helper T cell that coordinates the whole response. The drug classes above map onto that life cycle — entry inhibitors block CCR5, reverse transcriptase inhibitors block replication, protease inhibitors block assembly.

27

Oral manifestations of HIV

The worldwide list — and it is mostly this lecture's other diseases.

CategoryManifestations
Candidosis
(oral, with or without pharyngeal involvement)		Pseudomembranous, erythematous, hyperplastic, angular cheilitis
Oral hairy leukoplakiaEBV-related
Recurrent aphthous-like ulcerations 
Oral Kaposi’s sarcomaHHV-8
Oral herpes virusesSimplex and zoster
Human papillomavirus lesionsWart-like
Periodontal diseasesLinear gingival erythema; necrotising ulcerative gingivitis; necrotising ulcerative periodontitis
Read this list backwards

Almost every item is a disease from earlier in this lecture: all four candidal presentations, hairy leukoplakia (EBV), Kaposi’s sarcoma (HHV-8), herpes simplex and zoster, HPV warts, linear gingival erythema and necrotising ulcerative gingivitis. HIV does not cause a new set of diseases — it removes the restraint on the organisms already living in the mouth. That is the commensal-to-opportunist shift from section 2, at full scale.

Why the dentist is well placed

2,899 people in Australia were unaware they were HIV positive. Several of these lesions are visible on routine examination and require no special equipment. Recognising an unexpected combination — erythematous candidosis with hairy leukoplakia, or necrotising periodontitis in a young patient — is a reason for sensitive discussion and referral for testing.

Why do the oral manifestations of HIV consist almost entirely of diseases covered elsewhere in this lecture?

Because HIV causes CD4+ lymphocyte dysfunction, and the diseases that follow are opportunistic infections by organisms already present in the mouth. Candidosis, hairy leukoplakia (EBV), Kaposi’s sarcoma (HHV-8), herpes simplex and zoster and HPV lesions are all caused by commensals or latent viruses that a competent immune system holds in check. HIV does not introduce new organisms; it removes the restraint on existing ones.

28

Hepatitis C

Blood-borne, no vaccine — but now curable.

Incubation6–12 weeks
CourseAcute disease → chronic active hepatitis → cirrhosis → (hepatocellular carcinoma)
Chronic carriers100%
Chronic disease80%
Infected body fluidsBlood, saliva, semen
Needlestick risk~3%
VaccineNO VACCINE
Compare the needlestick numbers

Hepatitis C carries a ~3% seroconversion risk from a needlestick. Lecture 5C gave HIV at 0.3% — a tenfold difference, and hepatitis C has no vaccine and no post-exposure prophylaxis equivalent to PEP. For a dentist, HCV is the greater occupational risk of the two.

Oral findings in hepatitis C

  • Sjögren-like sialadenitis — 50% of individuals with HCV had salivary gland infiltration by lymphocytes, causing gland destruction and reduced salivary output
  • Xerostomia — 50% of individuals infected with HCV actually complained of dry mouth
  • Increased risk of salivary gland lymphoma
  • Association with lichen planus
  • ?Increased OSCC risk
  • Case reports — Behçet’s disease, vesiculobullous conditions
Sjögren-like, not Sjögren

Lecture 5B covered Sjögren syndrome as a CD4+ T cell reaction against ductal epithelium with SS-A (Ro) and SS-B (La) autoantibodies. HCV produces a histologically similar picture — lymphocytic infiltration destroying the gland — without being the same disease. A patient with unexplained xerostomia and lymphocytic sialadenitis needs HCV considered alongside Sjögren.

Hepatitis C can be cured

40–80% cure rates depending on genotype. Direct-acting antivirals now on the PBS include daclatasvir, sofosbuvir + velpatasvir, sofosbuvir + ledipasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, sofosbuvir, and sofosbuvir with velpatasvir and voxilaprevir.

A genuine change in prognosis

HCV is the one infection in this lecture where the outlook has recently been transformed. A disease that formerly progressed to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in most chronic carriers is now curable with an oral course — despite there still being no vaccine.

From the lecture slides
29

Summary and glossary

The whole lecture on one screen.

The through-line

  1. The mouth is a microbial habitat, not sterile
    >700 bacterial species, plus fungi and viruses.
  2. The question is what changed about the host
    Commensal versus opportunist; acute versus latent.
  3. Four groups
    Bacterial, prion, fungal, viral.
  4. Bacterial: three named diseases
    Actinomycosis (sulphur granules, lumpy jaw), syphilis (four stages), tuberculosis (acid-fast, granulomas).
  5. Candidosis has three forms
    Pseudomembranous wipes off; erythematous is red; hyperplastic will not wipe off and raises dysplasia.
  6. Treat the cause before the fungus
    Denture hygiene, inhaler rinsing, smoking cessation — then antifungals, watching the warfarin interaction.
  7. Herpesviruses become latent
    Up the nerve, silent in the ganglion, back down on reactivation.
  8. Vesicular infections sort on three questions
    Gingivae involved? Rash beyond the mouth? Does it recur?
  9. HPV: low-risk warts, high-risk oropharyngeal cancer
    90% of HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer is type 16; little role in the oral cavity proper.
  10. HIV removes restraint on what is already there
    Its oral manifestations are this lecture’s other diseases.

Glossary

Commensal
An organism living on the host without causing harm.
Opportunistic infection
Disease caused by an organism that is normally harmless, following a change in host defences.
Latent infection
Infection in which the organism persists silently and can reactivate later.
CPR group
Candidate Phyla Radiation — ultra-small bacteria of the oral microbiome.
Sulphur granules
Colonies of actinomyces and filaments surrounded by neutrophils; seen in actinomycosis.
Lumpy jaw
Nickname for actinomycosis — chronic soft tissue swelling becoming a hard, board-like, lumpy lesion.
Spirochaete
Spiral, motile organism with a central protoplasmic cylinder.
ANUG
Acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis; associated with T. vincentii.
Chancre
The primary lesion of syphilis; may involve tongue, gingivae or lips.
Mucous patches
Raised lesions with a pseudomembrane surrounded by erythema, in secondary syphilis.
Snail track ulceration
Serpiginous oral mucosal ulceration of secondary syphilis.
Gumma
Crater-type ulcer of tertiary syphilis that may involve bone, typically the hard palate.
Syphilitic leukoplakia
White patch of tertiary syphilis, reported as potentially malignant.
Acid fast
Resisting decolourisation by acid alcohol after staining; a property of mycobacteria due to mycolic acid.
Ziehl–Neelsen stain
Stain used to demonstrate acid-fast bacilli, since they do not take the Gram stain.
Prion
‘Proteinaceous infectious particle’, derived from a protease-sensitive normal cell membrane protein.
TSE
Transmissible spongiform encephalopathy — the family of prion diseases including CJD.
Saprophytism
Harmless carriage of a fungus, as opposed to pathogenicity.
Pseudomembrane
Mesh of fungal hyphae with desquamated epithelial cells, fibrin, keratin, necrotic tissue and bacteria; wipes off.
Erythematous candidosis
Localised red mucosa; formerly acute or chronic atrophic candidosis.
Chronic hyperplastic candidosis
Non-removable white plaque, formerly candidal leukoplakia; associated with epithelial dysplasia.
Chronic mucocutaneous candidosis
Genetic immune fault causing chronic candidosis of skin, nails and mucosae with autoimmune endocrinopathies.
Median rhomboid glossitis
Symmetrical rhomboid erythematous area of posterior dorsal tongue with atrophy of filiform papillae.
Linear gingival erythema
Non-plaque-induced gingivitis presenting as a 2–3 mm erythematous band along the gingival margin.
Invasive candidosis
Systemic candidal infection in the severely immunocompromised; high mortality.
Herpes labialis
Recurrent HSV-1 at mucocutaneous junctions; affects 30–40% of the population.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome
VZV reactivation involving the chorda tympani (VII), with ear vesicles, anterior tongue and soft palate lesions and facial palsy.
Post-herpetic neuralgia
Persistent neuropathic pain after shingles; affects >30% of patients.
Oral hairy leukoplakia
EBV-related bilateral epithelial proliferation of the tongue in immunosuppression.
Roseola infantum
Primary infection with HHV-6 or HHV-7; mild, self-limiting.
Herpangina
Coxsackie infection with vesicles of fauces, uvula, tonsils and palate; gingivae spared, no recurrence.
Koplik spots
Red spots with blue-white specks on the buccal mucosa, preceding the measles rash.
Heck’s disease
Multifocal epithelial hyperplasia, HPV 13 and 32; nodules appear to vanish when mucosa is stretched.
PrEP / PEP
Pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV; PEP is a 28-day course begun within 72 hours.
U=U
Undetectable equals untransmittable — no transmission from a virally suppressed partner.
Note on required reading

This lecture does not carry a single chapter reference in the way earlier lectures do; it draws on a wide primary literature, cited slide by slide (Kolenbrander 2002; McCullough 1996, 1997, 2002, 2005; Farah 2010; Williams & Lewis 2011; Samaranayake & Yaacob 1990; Baccaglini 2007; Carrozzo 2008; Anderson 2014, among others). Underwood’s Chapter 8 remains the background text for the immunological material it builds on.
